# Isaiah 12: Commentary Notes

**A note on sources:** My search and fetch budget ran out before I could get to the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, the netbible.org notes, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are therefore thin or missing. Where I name a teacher's tradition, it comes from your site list or the page itself.

---

## Before the verses: Who sings, and on what "day"?

This is where the traditions really differ, and the answer shapes how you read every verse.

- **Future Israel in the millennium (dispensational view).** Precept Austin quotes the KJV Bible Commentary, which reads the chapter literally as a song "speaking for the blessed millennial believers". In the same vein, it says the surviving remnant of Israel will praise God when the Messiah reigns. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_12_commentary
- J. Vernon McGee ties "that day" to the Great Tribulation and the kingdom that follows it. A.C. Gaebelein calls the chapter "Israel's future song of Praise for salvation". https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60580/
- Precept Austin still says "the truth of this promise is fully applicable to all believers". https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_12_commentary
- **The whole reign of Christ (Calvin).** Calvin says the song "is not limited to a short period, but, on the contrary, extends to the whole of Christ's reign". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/12.htm
- **Lutheran (1517.org, Jeffrey Pulse).** Pulse links "that day" to the second-coming language at the end of Isaiah 11, but admits scholars have reached no clear consensus. He preaches both the "now" of the Church and the "not yet" of the saints gathered in heaven. Isaiah 12 is also a canticle in the Lutheran Service Book (#927). https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-isaiah-121-6-lent-4-series-c
- **Both views noted.** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says some eminent commentators expect fulfilment only when the Jews are restored to their land. Others read the place-names as symbols of eternal truths. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-12.html
- **Pentecostal/charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik).** Guzik takes the song as coming from anyone who has surrendered to the Messiah as king and enjoys the benefits of His reign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/

---

## v. 1: "Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me"

**Traditional reading**
- Guzik: the worshipper *chooses* to praise God even after feeling His anger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/
- Matthew Henry: God's anger lasts only for a moment. It was turned away through Christ, "the root of Jesse," who is our peace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_012.cfm
- Precept Austin: this is the only mention of "comfort" in Isaiah 1–39. The verse moves from anger (the theme of chs. 1–39) to comfort (the theme of chs. 40–66). It also points out that "that day" was earlier something to dread, but here it is something to hope for. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_12_commentary
- Spurgeon (Baptist) stresses that the pronoun is singular: people receive peace one by one. Because God says "you *will* say," the promise cannot fail. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/a-new-song-for-new-hearts/

**Where traditions differ: is God angry with believers?**
- Guzik: God's wrath against us was "exhausted" on the cross. What believers feel now is fatherly discipline, which feels like anger but is love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/
- Calvin: this confession belongs only to the godly and elect. Their chastisements may look like those of the ungodly, but the reasons are very different. God's wrath against the ungodly is perpetual. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/12.htm

---

## v. 2: "God is my salvation… my strength and my song"

- Guzik: saying "God is my salvation" rejects the idea that our own works save us, and the verse repeats it for emphasis. "I will trust and not be afraid" is a decision of the will, not a feeling to wait for. He links this to Romans 5:1. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/
- Spurgeon, quoted by Precept Austin: calling God Himself "my salvation" means owing the whole of one's deliverance to the Lord. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_12_commentary
- Precept Austin: this is the first use in Isaiah of the Hebrew word for salvation, *yeshuah*. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60580/
- Calvin, quoted by Guzik: God is our *complete* strength, not just part of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/
- Matthew Henry: "Jah" is short for Jehovah, and both names speak of God's eternity and unchangeableness. Some take "Jah" to mean the Son of God made man. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_012.cfm
- Chuck Smith connects "Jehovah is salvation" with the name Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/12-6.html
- MacLaren: these words quote Moses' song at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:2). "Has become" points to one definite saving act in history, which he identifies with the Cross. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-3.htm

---

## v. 3: "With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation"

**Traditional reading**
- Ellicott: the verse may be part of the hymn, or addressed to those joining it; he prefers the second. He links it to the later Feast of Tabernacles ritual, when priests carried water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it at the altar. He notes the Talmud connects that act with Isaiah's words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-3.htm
- MacLaren: Jesus' cry in John 7:37 ("If any man thirst…") came at that water ceremony. The Hebrew means a *spring*, not a storage reservoir, and God Himself is the spring. "Drawing" means asking, coming, and believing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-3.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: salvation will be an inexhaustible well that everyone can draw from; compare John 4:14. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/12-3.htm
- Guzik: there are many wells, but all draw on one reservoir, Christ. That does not mean there are many ways to be saved. "Draw" shows we must act, yet the well, rope and bucket are all His. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/
- John Piper (desiringgod.org): the plural "wells" means supplies all along the journey. A well refills itself. Drinking at these wells is the key to missionaries persevering. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wells-of-salvation-and-the-work-of-missions

**Where traditions differ: what are the "wells"?**
- *Gospel ordinances and the Holy Spirit.* Benson says graces are drawn from God through gospel ordinances. He cites Bishop Lowth, who says the Jews took the water to mean the Holy Spirit's influences in the Messiah's days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-3.htm
- *Promises and the Spirit.* Trapp says the wells are the "words of eternal life," the precious promises, and the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/isaiah-12.html
- *Christ, drawn on by faith.* Gill says Christ is especially meant. Faith, which is God's gift, is the bucket, and it is used through prayer, Scripture, and the word and ordinances. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/isaiah/12-3.html
- *All three Persons.* Gill also says all three Persons of the Trinity are the fountain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/12-3.html
- *Lutheran: baptism.* Pulse suggests the saving and preserving water "could perhaps" be connected to baptism. https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-isaiah-121-6-lent-4-series-c

---

## v. 4: "Proclaim His name! Make His works known among the peoples"

- Keil & Delitzsch: this opens a second song in the tones of Psalm 105:1 and 1 Chronicles 16:8. "Call upon the name" here means to call it out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-6.htm
- Guzik: the living water now flows out to others. He quotes Trapp, who says the saints cannot praise enough on their own and so "call in help." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/
- Piper: "you will say" follows straight after drinking. The preaching that results is missionary preaching to the *peoples*. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-wells-of-salvation-and-the-work-of-missions
- Pulse: calling on the LORD's name also shows whom the people belong to. https://www.1517.org/articles/old-testament-isaiah-121-6-lent-4-series-c
- Dispensational reading (Precept Austin): believing Israel will finally fulfil its calling to the nations. "Make them remember" implies that even in the millennium, later generations may forget His name. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60580/

---

## v. 5: "Sing to the LORD… Let this be known in all the earth"

- Keil & Delitzsch: this is a wish that all humanity would come to know God's glorious self-revelation. When God redeems His people, He has every nation's salvation in view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-6.htm
- Calvin: the glorious work is that God sent His Son to reconcile us and destroy the power of death and the devil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/12.htm
- Guzik: if the Lord is your song, sing it, with energy rather than mechanical routine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-12/

---

## v. 6: "Great among you is the Holy One of Israel"

- Ellicott and Pulpit: "inhabitant" is feminine in Hebrew and stands for the whole community. Ellicott notes that the hymn ends with Isaiah's characteristic name for God and closes the "Immanuel volume" of his prophecies. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/12-6.htm
- Pulpit: the Church's crowning glory is her Lord's presence among her, which is continuous, effective, yet invisible. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/12-6.htm
- Calvin: our only true happiness is God dwelling among us. By addressing Zion, Isaiah also urges unity of faith with the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/12-6.html
- Gill: the Holy One is Christ, Redeemer and Husband of the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/12-6.html
- Matthew Henry: God is "great, because holy." He applies Zion to the gospel church, with Christ as Zion's King. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/12-6.html
- Geneva Study Bible: "You who are of the Church." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/isaiah-12.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, by contrast, takes "in the midst of thee" to mean literally Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/12-6.htm

---

## Other views (limited)

- **Modern scholarship:** Coffman reports that earlier critics rejected the song as not Isaiah's. Peake called it "a late appendix". Coffman says such claims had lost most of their appeal by 1937. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/12-6.html
- **Translation differences (v. 6):** the NET Bible has "the Holy One of Israel acts mightily among you." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/12-6.htm
- **Translation differences (v. 3):** the Catholic Douay-Rheims has "out of the saviour's fountains." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/isaiah/12-3.html
- **Not found:** I did not reach any Catholic or Orthodox commentary, and I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
